{
  "body": "The situation has four threads that are easy to tangle and worth separating, because each points at a different lever.

First, the recurring arguments themselves: ordinary chore disputes between friends usually carry accumulated fairness perceptions, so the visible fight is often not really about the chore in question. Second, the agreements that later mean different things: this pattern suggests the agreements are vague ('I'll sort the kitchen'), unrecorded, and measured against different private standards of what 'done' looks like. That is a conjecture rather than a diagnosis, but it is cheap to test: write down the next few agreements with a task, an owner, a definition of done, and a deadline, and see whether the same disputes recur. Third, the changing work schedules: any allocation tuned to this month's timetables will keep breaking, so a fixed rota is the wrong shape; a rotation, or standing ownership with an explicit swap rule, degrades more gracefully. Fourth, the friend who now avoids the conversations: avoidance is usually about the felt cost of the talk — conflict, repetition, futility — rather than about any particular chore, so the lever is to make the conversation cheaper. Written or asynchronous coordination, shorter and rarer meetings, or a low-stakes one-on-one that asks what format they could tolerate before asking anything about chores are all ways to do that.

One further conjecture changes what an 'agreement' even is here: flatmates often differ in their threshold for when a chore needs doing, and the person who notices first ends up either doing it or nagging. Negotiating minimum shared standards is a separate conversation from dividing the labor, and conflating the two generates arguments that no rota can fix.

For the person asking what to do: they control the proposal, the record-keeping, and the approach to the avoider; they do not control the other two's standards or goodwill. A concrete package worth proposing is a two-to-four-week trial of a written shared note (task, owner, definition of done, deadline, swap rule), a ten-minute weekly check-in, and a separate one-on-one with the avoiding friend. Whether visible tracking reassures or inflames a friendship is genuinely unclear and should be watched during the trial rather than assumed either way.",
  "commitments": "Taking this account up means treating its conjectures as revisable, not established. The ambiguity conjecture stands or falls with a simple test: record the next few agreements in writing with task, owner, definition of done, and deadline; if disputes recur anyway, the conjecture weakens and attention should shift to the differing-standards thread or to accumulated resentment, which this account keeps separate. The proposed actions are a written shared record, a short trial of a rotation or swap-based arrangement with explicit rebalancing rules, a brief recurring check-in, and a one-on-one with the avoiding friend aimed at making the conversations cheaper rather than at any specific chore. These carry stated risks: a visible ledger between friends can produce scorekeeping and may inflame rather than reassure, and whether tracking helps this particular group is left unresolved pending the trial. The advice depends on all three flatmates being willing to try something; if the avoider refuses every format, the problem changes shape — toward whether the living arrangement is viable — and this account does not cover that case. Scope is limited to ordinary chore conflict between friends; if the arguments are carrying a deeper rupture in the friendship, a different account is needed.
